title: Multiply by 11 in your head—without forgetting the carry
description: 34 × 11 is friendly. 78 × 11 reveals the catch. Work through both, then try three short calculations of your own.
practice: Once the examples feel comfortable, try Math Rush. It mixes arithmetic questions, so choose a useful method rather than forcing the eleven trick onto every problem.

sections.title: Eleven is ten plus one
sections.html:
To multiply a number by 11, multiply it by 10 and add the original number. For 34, that is 340 + 34 = 374. This method works even when a clever-looking digit shortcut feels harder to remember than the calculation.

Picture eleven boxes, each holding 34 counters. Ten boxes contain 340; one more contains 34. You are adding groups you already understand.

sections.title: Where the middle-digit trick comes from
sections.html:
For a two-digit number such as 34, keep the outer digits and add them to make the middle: 3, then 3 + 4, then 4. The result is 374.

That pattern comes from place value, not coincidence. Write 340 above 34 with the units aligned. The hundreds column has 3, the tens column has 4 + 3, and the units column has 4. Because the middle sum is less than ten, no carrying is needed.

Try 52 × 11 the same way: 5, then 7, then 2. Check with 520 + 52 = 572.

sections.title: The catch: what happens with 78?
sections.html:
Seven plus eight is 15. You cannot squeeze 15 into a single digit position and call the answer 7158.

  1. Keep 8 in the units place.
  2. Put the 5 from 15 in the tens place.
  3. Carry the remaining 1 into the hundreds: 7 + 1 = 8.

So 78 × 11 = 858. The longer check is 780 + 78 = 858. If you forget the carry, go back to that addition; there is no need to abandon the problem.

sections.title: Three examples, with one deliberate trap
sections.html:
Work out 23 × 11, 67 × 11 and 99 × 11. Take your time with the last one: carrying can create an extra digit.

Compare your answers
  • 23 × 11 = 253: 230 + 23.
  • 67 × 11 = 737: 670 + 67.
  • 99 × 11 = 1089: 990 + 99.

For 99, the middle sum is 18. Put 8 in the tens place and carry 1 into the 9 hundreds. Ten hundreds becomes one thousand. That is why the answer has four digits.

sections.title: Use the method that costs you less effort
sections.html:
For 126 × 11, ten-times-plus-one is still straightforward: 1260 + 126 = 1386. The simple two-digit shortcut above should not be applied unchanged to a three-digit number.

The underlying idea is the distributive property: splitting 11 into 10 + 1 does not change the result. Learn that idea once and you can also turn multiplication by 9 into ten times the number minus one copy. For example, 34 × 9 = 340 − 34 = 306.
